interactions.label: Secretory diarrhoea resolves when the patient fasts, because no further substrat

params.question: Secretory diarrhoea resolves when the patient fasts, because no further substrate enters the gut.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This describes osmotic diarrhoea, not secretory. Secretory diarrhoea is driven by active ion secretion into the lumen (e.g. cholera toxin → cAMP → CFTR activation) and continues regardless of oral intake. Osmotic diarrhoea resolves with fasting because the unabsorbed solute is no longer entering the gut.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Secretory diarrhoea persists even during fasting because it is driven by active chloride secretion (e.g. cholera toxin activating cAMP-mediated CFTR channels), independent of luminal contents. It is osmotic diarrhoea that resolves with fasting, since it depends on an unabsorbed solute such as lactose.

params.question: A 40-year-old man presents to a district hospital with acute diarrhoea. Which aspect of the clinical evaluation should be prioritised FIRST?

answers.text: Detailed dietary history over the past 72 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dietary history is important for identifying the source but comes after ensuring the patient is haemodynamically stable. Dehydration is the immediate life-threatening complication.
Stool examination guides specific treatment but follows the initial clinical assessment and stabilisation of the patient.

Dehydration is the immediate threat in acute diarrhoea. Assessing severity — pulse, blood pressure, skin turgor, mental status, urine output — determines whether the patient needs urgent intravenous fluids or can be managed with oral rehydration.

answers.text: Sexual history to assess for specific pathogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sexual history is relevant in certain populations (e.g. men who have sex with men, HIV-positive patients) but is not the first priority in acute diarrhoea assessment.

overallFeedback.feedback: In acute diarrhoea, always assess dehydration severity first. A postural blood pressure drop can signal significant volume loss before the patient appears critically unwell. This determines whether the patient needs Plan A (home ORS), Plan B (supervised oral rehydration), or Plan C (immediate IV fluids).
Exactly. Dehydration assessment comes first because it determines the immediacy and route of rehydration — the single most important intervention in acute diarrhoea.

interactions.label: On stool microscopy of a patient with acute watery diarrhoea, faecal leucocytes

params.question: On stool microscopy of a patient with acute watery diarrhoea, faecal leucocytes are absent. What does this finding indicate about the diarrhoeal mechanism?

answers.text: The diarrhoea is inflammatory with mucosal invasion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inflammatory diarrhoea characteristically shows faecal leucocytes due to mucosal invasion and neutrophil infiltration. Their absence argues against an invasive process.

answers.text: The process is non-invasive — secretory or osmotic rather than inflammatory

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Absence of faecal leucocytes indicates an intact mucosa. In secretory diarrhoea (e.g. cholera) and osmotic diarrhoea, the epithelium is not invaded. Their presence would point to inflammatory causes such as Shigella or Entamoeba histolytica.

answers.text: The patient definitely has a viral aetiology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While viral gastroenteritis is non-invasive and would lack faecal leucocytes, other non-invasive causes (cholera, ETEC, osmotic diarrhoea) also show absent leucocytes. The finding indicates the mechanism, not the specific aetiology.

answers.text: Stool culture is unnecessary and should not be ordered

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The decision to send a stool culture depends on clinical indications — dysentery, duration beyond 7 days, suspected outbreaks, or immunocompromise — not solely on the presence or absence of faecal leucocytes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Faecal leucocytes are present when the intestinal mucosa is invaded (inflammatory diarrhoea) and absent when it is intact (secretory or osmotic diarrhoea). This single finding tells you the mechanism and guides your differential diagnosis.
Correct. Faecal leucocytes are the microscopic marker of mucosal invasion. Their absence points to a secretory or osmotic mechanism, narrowing your differential before any culture result.

interactions.label: A 22-year-old man presents with profuse rice-water stools and severe dehydration

params.question: A 22-year-old man presents with profuse rice-water stools and severe dehydration during a cholera outbreak. After initiating intravenous Ringer's Lactate, which antibiotic is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice for Shigella dysentery, which presents with bloody mucoid stools and tenesmus — not the watery, rice-water pattern seen in cholera.

answers.text: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral vancomycin is reserved for Clostridioides difficile infection, typically following recent antibiotic use. It has no role in cholera management.

In cholera, doxycycline (300 mg single dose) is the adjunctive antibiotic of choice. It reduces the duration and volume of diarrhoea. Rehydration remains the primary life-saving intervention; the antibiotic is adjunctive only because cholera is toxin-mediated.

Azithromycin is used for traveller's diarrhoea caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli. While it can be an alternative in cholera in some settings, single-dose doxycycline is the standard first-line choice.

overallFeedback.feedback: In cholera, doxycycline 300 mg as a single dose is the adjunctive antibiotic of choice. Remember the mechanistic split: cholera is toxin-mediated (doxycycline adjunctive), Shigella is invasive (ciprofloxacin essential), and C. difficile requires stopping the precipitating antibiotic and starting oral vancomycin.
Correct. Cholera is toxin-mediated, so doxycycline is adjunctive — rehydration is the definitive treatment. The single-dose regimen reduces stool output and shortens illness duration.

interactions.label: After treating invasive intestinal amoebiasis with metronidazole, what is the es

params.question: After treating invasive intestinal amoebiasis with metronidazole, what is the essential next step?

answers.text: Repeat stool microscopy at 48 hours to confirm clearance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Follow-up microscopy is useful but is not the critical next step. Without a luminal agent, cysts persist in the intestinal lumen even after trophozoites are eliminated, leading to relapse and continued transmission.
Albendazole is used for helminthic infections (roundworms, hookworms, whipworms). It has no role in eliminating Entamoeba histolytica cyst carriage.

answers.text: Prescribe a luminal agent such as diloxanide furoate or paromomycin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metronidazole eliminates invasive trophozoites but does not clear cysts from the intestinal lumen. A luminal agent (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) is mandatory to eradicate cyst carriage, preventing both relapse and ongoing faecal-oral transmission. This is the most commonly missed step in amoebiasis treatment.
Nitazoxanide is the agent of choice for Cryptosporidium parvum, not for follow-up treatment of amoebiasis. The correct follow-up is a luminal cysticidal agent.

overallFeedback.feedback: After metronidazole for invasive amoebiasis, always follow with a luminal agent (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) to eliminate cyst carriage. Metronidazole kills trophozoites in tissue but leaves cysts in the gut lumen intact — without this step, relapse and transmission continue.

Exactly right. The two-step treatment of amoebiasis — tissue amoebicide (metronidazole) followed by luminal amoebicide (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) — is essential to prevent relapse and transmission.
